The timing of puberty is not uniform across all individuals; in a captive study, only 2 out of 7 individuals had reached this stage by 17 months, suggesting significant inter-individual variation in the pace of maturation.

Upon reaching sexual maturity, female hyraxes continue to grow toward their ultimate adult mass. The maximum recorded wet body mass for a fully grown adult is 4000 grams [Wwi = 4000 grams], a figure that represents the asymptotic body size for the species under optimal conditions. This ultimate mass is considerably larger than the mass at puberty, highlighting that somatic growth does not cease with the onset of reproductive capability. The combination of a high birth mass, a delayed puberty, and a long lifespan positions Procavia capensis as a textbook example of a slow-living, precocial mammal adapted to the stable, resource-limited environments of the African savanna and rocky outcrops.
